soil-agri-082.title: Soil survey: putting an area's soils on the map
soil-agri-082.text: For decades, a US county's soil survey arrived as a printed book, and it could take years to publish. A soil survey, also called soil mapping, classifies the soil types and other soil properties of an area and records where each one lies. It applies soil science and draws heavily on geomorphology, physical geography, patterns of vegetation and land use, and theories of {{ref:soil-form-042}}. Its primary data come from field sampling and from remote sensing, mainly aerial photography. LiDAR and other digital techniques are steadily gaining ground. In the second half of the 20th century, soil mapping meant field survey and drawing soil-type boundaries by hand. Map scales varied by country and purpose. Surveyors carried paper air photos, topographic maps and mapping keys. Many now carry a rugged tablet with GPS, digital imagery, LiDAR and soil geodatabases. In the United States, the program described in {{ref:soil-hist-051}} once published a book for each county. A typical county survey held a general map of soils and a detailed map of indexed soil series. It added a section on soil use and management, and tables of land-use suitability. Today surveys appear on the web through Web Soil Survey, run by the federal agency known as the NRCS, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-050}}. There users build custom surveys, and changes go live in moments. The agency has maps and data online for more than 95 percent of US counties.

soil-agri-084.title: The soil map, from hand-drawn polygons to predicted grids
soil-agri-084.text: Farmers who practice precision agriculture read soil maps to adjust what they put on each field. A soil map shows where soil types lie across an area, or how properties such as pH, texture, organic matter or horizon depth vary. It is usually the product of a soil survey. Traditional maps show only the general distribution of soils and accompany the survey report. Some maps are hand-drawn polygons of soil types. Others predict or simulate soil properties in two or three dimensions, or predict soil classes. Maps of primary attributes show what was described or measured in the field. Maps of secondary, inferred attributes show properties for a use, such as production capacity or degradation. Most maps serve land evaluation, spatial planning, agricultural extension and environmental protection. Many new ones come from {{ref:soil-agri-089}}. They show more detail but are not necessarily more accurate, though statistical maps can include an estimate of their own uncertainty.

soil-agri-088.title: Prime farmland: the best soils, and the cities on them
soil-agri-088.text: Many cities grew up in rich farming country, so the best land for crops is often well suited to houses too. The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) calls the best of it prime farmland. This land has the best combination of physical and chemical characteristics for producing food, feed, forage, fiber and oilseed crops, and it is still available for those uses. Its soil quality, growing season and moisture supply give economically sustained high yields under acceptable farming methods, including water management. It generally has a dependable water supply and a favorable temperature and growing season. Its acidity or alkalinity is acceptable, as is its salt and sodium content, and it has few or no rocks. It is not excessively erodible or long saturated with water. It either rarely floods or is protected from flooding. The designation helps growth management keep such land farmed, through zoning, conservation easements and green belts. Three USDA designations complement it: farmland of statewide importance, farmland of local importance and unique farmland. Unique farmland is used for specific high-value crops such as nuts, olives, cranberries and citrus. State and local agencies set the criteria for the statewide and local categories in cooperation with the USDA. Preserving prime soils is hard where they cover less than 60% of an area. A universal way to mark them out, joining science and policy, is still needed.

soil-agri-087.title: Germany's soil value, scored from 0 to 100
soil-agri-087.text: Germany's soil value, or Bodenwertzahl, rates soil quality from 0, very low, to 100, very high. For arable land it combines field assessments of soil type, soil development and parent material. It expresses the soil's relative net income under proper management. Heavy to clayey loams score 31–50, partly loess-covered loams 51–70 and loess-covered loams 71–90. Adjusting for terrain, climate and location gives the field value, or Ackerzahl. It began with the Reich Soil Assessment under the 1934 Soil Assessment Act, which set a Magdeburg Börde farm at 100 for farm tax ratings. A record 102.8 was later measured near Hildesheim.

soil-agri-089.title: Digital soil mapping hands the pen to computers
soil-agri-089.text: ISRIC's SoilGrids maps cover the whole globe at 250 m resolution, and machine learning drew them. They are a product of digital soil mapping, also called predictive soil mapping: the computer-assisted production of maps of soil types and soil properties. The Working Group on Digital Soil Mapping defines it as building geographically referenced soil databases at a set resolution. Field and laboratory observations are linked to environmental data by quantitative relationships. In traditional mapping, field soil scientists draw boundaries by hand, though those maps can also be digitized. Digital mapping relies on GPS, field scanners and remote sensing, plus geostatistical interpolation, GIS, digital elevation models and data mining. It tries to overcome old maps that often only outline soil classes, offer no basis for modeling changing soil, and resist quantitative study of soil function. Semi-automated methods lower costs. The products are routinely checked for accuracy and uncertainty, and they are easier to update as new data arrive. EU maps of texture and bulk density, for example, rest on about 20,000 LUCAS topsoil samples.

soil-agri-083.title: Reading a soil survey for farms, buildings and gardens
soil-agri-083.text: Survey data are of little use to a planner until someone interprets them. Soil survey interpretation uses survey information to predict the potentials and limitations of soils for particular uses, such as crops, building or gardens. Farmers and ranchers learn whether a soil suits crops or livestock and what management it needs. Architects and engineers use soil engineering properties to judge construction sites. The predictions guide land use and management on areas from small tracts to several million acres. They must still be weighed with economic, social and environmental considerations before becoming valid land-use recommendations. Published US surveys include land-use suitability tables based on NRCS standards.

soil-found-069.title: The European Soil Database, one grid for a continent
soil-found-069.text: Europe has only one harmonized soil database, and many other soil data, information and services draw on it. The European Soil Database is based on experts' knowledge. The European Commission's LUCAS topsoil survey adds sampled soil data across the European Union. Its v2 Raster Library holds public-domain grids of 1 km x 1 km cells, aligned with the INSPIRE reference grid. They cover texture, parent material, WRB soil type, soil depth, mineralogy, cation exchange capacity and available water capacity. Combined with land cover, climate and topography data, it gives the most homogeneous data on the organic carbon content of European soils.

soil-agri-086.title: SSURGO, the database behind US soil surveys
soil-agri-086.text: The soil surveys that once filled county books now sit in a database. SSURGO, the Soil Survey Geographic database, is digital soil data produced and distributed by the NRCS. It is the dataset in which the NRCS maintains its soil information. It records soil types and where they occur, their characteristics and properties, and their limits, risks and suitability for various uses. Its data reach users through Web Soil Survey, which the NRCS runs as the single authoritative source of US soil survey information.

soil-agri-092.title: Pedometrics: measuring soil with mathematics
soil-agri-092.text: The name says it plainly: the Greek pedos, 'soil', joined to metron, 'measurement'. Pedometrics applies mathematical and statistical methods to the distribution and genesis of soils. It is a sub-discipline of pedology focused on quantitative techniques, especially for mapping soil properties. It tackles soil problems clouded by deterministic or random variation, vagueness and lack of knowledge. Its simulation models build on chaos theory, statistical distributions or fuzzy logic. Its advance is tied to better remote and close-range sensing, and to wavelets, fuzzy sets and data mining.

soil-agri-091.title: Pedometric mapping turns soil into continuous grids
soil-agri-091.text: A traditional surveyor infers soil bodies from a mental model and draws them by hand. The result is subjective and hard to test for accuracy without extra sampling. Pedometric mapping, also called statistical soil mapping, produces soil property and soil class maps from data by statistical methods. It works largely through geostatistics, the statistics of data spread across space. It predicts soil variables at unsampled places and estimates the uncertainty of each prediction. Its outputs come from rigorous statistical computing, so they are reproducible. Traditional mapping shows soil types as discrete bodies on polygon maps. Pedometric mapping shows measured properties as continuous grids, with maps of prediction error. Unlike {{ref:soil-agri-089}} as a whole, it relies strictly on geostatistics and draws no discrete soil types. It leans on detailed covariate layers, maps of other variables such as elevation-model derivatives, remote sensing imagery, climate, land cover and geology. The aim is practical: predicting how a soil-plant ecosystem will respond to management.

soil-agri-093.title: Matheron's three-part model of soil variation
soil-agri-093.text: Every soil measurement hides three parts. The universal model of soil variation writes a soil variable as Z(s) = m(s) + ε′(s) + ε″. The three parts are a deterministic trend, a spatially autocorrelated random part and leftover noise. Spatially autocorrelated means nearby values are related. French mathematician Georges Matheron introduced the model, and it has proven the best unbiased linear predictor for spatial data. Regression-kriging, also called universal kriging, uses it to predict or simulate soils. The trend is often modeled from the classic soil-forming factors: climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, the CLORPT model.

soil-agri-094.title: The Storie index, where one zero sinks the score
soil-agri-094.text: Multiply a string of ratings together, and a single zero wipes out all the rest. That is the logic of the Storie index, a soil rating method based on the soil characteristics that govern a land's potential use and productive capacity. R. Earl Storie developed it at the University of California, Berkeley, in the 1930s for land valuation, independent of other physical or economic factors. It rates soil depth and texture, permeability, chemical characteristics, drainage and runoff, and climate where climate is not uniform. Its ratings are subjective, and O'Geen and colleagues updated the method in 2008 to reduce this.

soil-agri-090.title: Scorpan: seven letters for predicting soil
soil-agri-090.text: Seven letters hold the whole idea: S = f(s,c,o,r,p,a,n). The scorpan model predicts a soil class or attribute from soil, climate, organisms, relief, parent material, age and position. It adapts the five classic soil-forming factors, but for a different job. It does not explain how soil forms. It describes, empirically, how soil relates to other mapped factors. Two letters are new: s stands for soil properties already measured at a point, and n for spatial or geographic position. These relationships serve as soil spatial prediction functions for {{ref:soil-agri-089}}.

soil-agri-085.title: Soil information systems hold the whole inventory
soil-agri-085.text: Behind every digital soil map sits a larger store of data. A soil information system is a systematic, consistent collection of gridded or vector maps of soil properties and classes. It covers a whole area of interest and comes with a report, manual or metadata. Digital soil maps are visualizations of the soil inventories it stores, and its major part is a soil geographical database. Most systems combine polygon and point maps linked to attribute tables for profile observations, soil mapping units and soil classes. ISRIC works to strengthen national, regional and continental systems, and a new global one is being developed under the initiative described in {{ref:soil-env-190}}.

openers.soil-survey-and-land-evaluation: Knowing a soil is only half the work; someone must also record where it lies. This chapter starts with the soil survey, which classifies an area's soils and records them geographically, and with the soil map it produces. It then turns to judging land: predicting what soils can and cannot do for crops, building or gardens, and rating them, as the US Department of Agriculture does with {{ref:soil-agri-088}} and Germany does on a scale from 0 to 100. The last stretch moves to computers, from {{ref:soil-agri-089}} and national soil databases to the mathematics of soil variation.

reviews.soil-survey-and-land-evaluation: A soil survey classifies an area's soils and records where they lie, and its usual product is a soil map. Interpretation turns that map into predictions of what land can do, while ratings such as prime farmland, the German soil value and the Storie index rank it for crops, taxes or valuation. Paper county books have given way to databases such as SSURGO and the European Soil Database, held within soil information systems. Digital soil mapping, pedometrics and pedometric mapping now predict soil from data, using Matheron's model and the scorpan relationships. Their maps are reproducible and can carry an estimate of their own uncertainty, which hand-drawn boundaries are hard to test for.
